title: The Spin-Network Reservoir
intro: The founding QRC model (Fujii and Nakajima 2017) is a few qubits with random all-to-all XX couplings and a Z field, fed by resetting one qubit to an input-dependent state each step and read out through single-qubit Z expectations. This page builds it completely, step by step with numbers, explains why it remembers and forgets, and runs it.

blocks.text: What you need first

The two-qubit reservoir in A Quantum Reservoir Worked by Hand (#/qrc/start/quantum-reservoir-by-hand) (the density matrix of a two-qubit state, the partial trace, one step of evolution) and the idea of a ridge readout from Linear Regression and the Ridge Readout (#/qrc/start/linear-regression-and-ridge). From the Quantum Mechanics shelf: Pauli Operators and Rotations (#/quantum/qubits/pauli-and-rotations), Composite Systems and Tensor Products (#/quantum/many-body/composite-systems), Mixed States (#/quantum/many-body/mixed-states) and The Schrödinger Equation (#/quantum/dynamics/schrodinger-equation). Symmetries and Conservation (#/quantum/dynamics/symmetries-and-conservation) helps for the parity section but is explained again where it is used.
What you will be able to do

items: Write down the Hamiltonian of the spin-network reservoir, count its random parameters, and say what each of the two terms does and what happens if you remove either.
Carry one input step by hand for a two-qubit reservoir: discard qubit 1, insert the input state, evolve, and read the features, with the numbers checked against a program.
Prove that the Hamiltonian conserves the parity $Z_1Z_2\cdots Z_n$ and say what that means for which observables can respond to which parts of the state.
Explain where the memory comes from, why the reset is the only forgetting mechanism, and which time scales set how long the memory is.
Run the full model (several qubits, virtual nodes, ridge readout) and read its memory function and memory capacity.

blocks.text: What the model is, in one paragraph

The spin-network reservoir was proposed by Keisuke Fujii and Kohei Nakajima in 2017 and is the model against which almost every later quantum reservoir is compared. It has a handful of qubits (spin-1/2 particles) that all interact with each other through fixed random couplings and sit in a magnetic field. The input is a number $s_k$ between 0 and 1 arriving once per time step. At the start of each step qubit 1 is thrown away and replaced with a fresh qubit whose state depends on $s_k$; then the whole register is left alone to evolve for a fixed time $\Delta t$; then the average value of $Z$ on each qubit is recorded. Those averages are the features, and a ridge regression turns them into the answer. Nothing in the spin network is ever trained.

Every ingredient has a job. The couplings spread whatever was written on qubit 1 across the other qubits. The field makes the qubits precess, which is what turns a population difference into a coherence and back, and so mixes the information. The reset writes the input and, at the same time, is the only place information is ever destroyed. The rest of this page builds each ingredient from a question you can feel, and ends with a program you can run.
The Hamiltonian
Why we need it

A reservoir has two jobs that pull in opposite directions. It must keep the input around for a while, so it needs something that stores. And it must spread the input over many features, so a single linear readout can pick out different parts of the history, so it needs something that mixes. A single isolated qubit stores perfectly and mixes nothing: whatever you write on it stays on it. The question is the simplest set of interactions that makes a few qubits store and mix at once.
The idea in plain words

Take $n$ qubits. Every pair of qubits is coupled by an interaction of the form (strength)$\times X_iX_j$, with a strength chosen at random once and then frozen. And every qubit sits in a field along $Z$. The coupling term is the one that moves information between qubits; the field term is the one that makes each qubit's state rotate about the $z$ axis at its own pace.

An everyday picture: a set of tuning forks on one table, each connected to every other by a rubber band of a different stiffness. Strike one, and the energy leaks along the bands into the others, comes back, leaks out again; at any moment each fork holds a different mixture of the history of the strike. The picture breaks in one important way: the forks are classical and their motion is a smooth wave, whereas the qubits carry amplitudes, and what you read out is an average over many repetitions of a quantum measurement.
The maths, one step at a time
The Hamiltonian is

blocks.tex: H = \sum_{i<j} J_{ij}\, X_i X_j + \sum_{i} h_i\, Z_i, \qquad J_{ij} \sim \mathcal{U}\!\left[-\tfrac{J}{2}, \tfrac{J}{2}\right], \quad h_i = h + \delta_i,\ \delta_i \sim \mathcal{U}\!\left[-\tfrac{W}{2},\tfrac{W}{2}\right]
blocks.caption: The Fujii–Nakajima Hamiltonian has a uniform field; the site disorder W is added on this shelf and in its simulators to explore the dynamical regimes (the next pages).

blocks.text: Read the symbols one at a time. $X_i$ means the Pauli operator $X$ acting on qubit $i$ and the identity on every other qubit; so $X_iX_j$ is a product that flips qubit $i$ and qubit $j$ together. The sum over $i<j$ runs over every pair once: $n(n-1)/2$ pairs. $J_{ij}$ is the strength of the coupling of that pair. The notation $\mathcal{U}[-J/2, J/2]$ means a number drawn uniformly at random from that interval; in all the numerical work here $J=1$, so each coupling is a random number between $-0.5$ and $0.5$. The field term gives qubit $i$ the energy $h_i Z_i$; $h$ is the common field strength and $\delta_i$ is a small random offset of width $W$ that is zero unless we ask for disorder. We use the shelf convention $\hbar = 1$, so energies are rates: a field $h$ makes the qubit precess at angular frequency $2h$.

For $n=4$ qubits that is $6$ random couplings and $4$ fields: ten numbers, which are fixed for the life of the reservoir, define a $16\times16$ matrix. Nothing about those numbers is tuned. They are the physics of the device.
What each term does by itself

items: Remove the field ($h=0$, $W=0$). Every $X_iX_j$ commutes with every other $X_kX_l$ (they are all built from $X$ operators, and $X$ commutes with $X$). So all the terms can be made diagonal at the same time, in the basis of eigenstates of the $X_i$. The time evolution is then just a set of independent phases, one for each of the $2^n$ basis states, with no mixing between those states. The reservoir is integrable, its dynamics is a sum of simple oscillations, and it does not scramble information. The Dynamical Regimes (#/qrc/models/dynamical-regimes) page makes this precise.

Remove the couplings ($J=0$). Each qubit precesses alone, and nothing ever leaves qubit 1. The reset throws away everything written there and the other qubits see no input at all. The reservoir has no memory.

Keep both. The field makes the single-qubit eigenbasis ($Z$) differ from the eigenbasis of the coupling ($X$), so the two terms do not commute and the dynamics mixes. Random couplings break any symmetry that swaps qubits, so the system is generic, apart from one exact symmetry that we meet below.

blocks.text: A worked example: two qubits

Take $n=2$, one coupling $J_{12}=J$ and a uniform field $h$: $H = J\,X_1X_2 + h(Z_1+Z_2)$. Use the basis $\vert00\rangle,\vert01\rangle,\vert10\rangle,\vert11\rangle$ (the leftmost digit is qubit 1). $X_1X_2$ flips both digits, so it connects $\vert00\rangle\leftrightarrow\vert11\rangle$ and $\vert01\rangle\leftrightarrow\vert10\rangle$ with amplitude $J$, and nothing else. $Z_1+Z_2$ is diagonal: it equals $+2$ on $\vert00\rangle$, $0$ on $\vert01\rangle$ and $\vert10\rangle$, and $-2$ on $\vert11\rangle$. The $4\times4$ matrix therefore splits into two independent $2\times2$ blocks.

items: Block A, on $\{\vert00\rangle,\vert11\rangle\}$. Row 1: $(2h,\ J)$. Row 2: $(J,\ -2h)$.
Block B, on $\{\vert01\rangle,\vert10\rangle\}$. Row 1: $(0,\ J)$. Row 2: $(J,\ 0)$.

blocks.text: A matrix with rows $(a, J)$ and $(J, -a)$ has eigenvalues $\pm\sqrt{a^2+J^2}$ (the sum of eigenvalues is the trace 0, and their product is the determinant $-a^2-J^2$). So block A has eigenvalues $\pm\Omega$ with $\Omega=\sqrt{4h^2+J^2}$, and block B has $\pm J$. With $h=1$ and $J=0.5$: $\Omega=\sqrt{4.25}=2.0616$, and the four energies are $-2.0616,\,-0.5,\,0.5,\,2.0616$; the program below prints exactly those.

What does this say about motion? Start in $\vert00\rangle$ (both qubits up in $Z$). It lives in block A, which is a two-level system with a large diagonal term $2h$ and a small coupling $J$. The probability of ever reaching $\vert11\rangle$ is at most $J^2/\Omega^2=0.25/4.25=0.059$. This is the standard result for a two-level system with an energy mismatch: a strong field detunes the pair-flip. Start instead in $\vert10\rangle$ (one flip). It lives in block B, whose diagonal is $0$: the two states $\vert10\rangle$ and $\vert01\rangle$ have the same energy, so the excitation hops completely, $P=\sin^2(Jt)$, back and forth. Hopping between equal-energy states is what carries information between qubits; pair creation is mostly suppressed by the field. This distinction (hopping that conserves $Z$-parity of the pair, pair creation that costs energy) returns on the Dynamical Regimes (#/qrc/models/dynamical-regimes) page.

Common confusion: the Hamiltonian has no explicit time dependence. The input does not change $H$. The input changes the state of qubit 1 at the start of each step, and then the same fixed $H$ acts. The reservoir is a fixed machine; only its contents change.

blocks.title: Check yourself: block energies
blocks.text: With $h=0.5$ and $J=0.3$ on two qubits, find the eigenvalues of the block on $\{\vert00\rangle,\vert11\rangle\}$ and the largest probability of reaching $\vert11\rangle$ starting from $\vert00\rangle$.
blocks.hint: The eigenvalues of a $2\times2$ block with diagonal $\pm a$ and off-diagonal $J$ are $\pm\sqrt{a^2+J^2}$.
solution: Block A has rows $(2h, J)=(1, 0.3)$ and $(0.3, -1)$.

blocks.text: The parity symmetry
Why we need it

In the two-qubit example the matrix fell into two separate blocks. That was not an accident of $n=2$, and it matters in practice: it decides which observables can see which parts of the state, which encodings work (the Input Encoding (#/qrc/models/input-encoding) page), and how to test whether a reservoir is chaotic (the Dynamical Regimes (#/qrc/models/dynamical-regimes) page). The question: is there a quantity that the Hamiltonian never changes?
The idea

Each $Z_i$ has eigenvalue $+1$ for a qubit in $\vert0\rangle$ and $-1$ for a qubit in $\vert1\rangle$. Their product $\Pi = Z_1Z_2\cdots Z_n$ is $+1$ if an even number of qubits are in $\vert1\rangle$ and $-1$ if an odd number are. It is a parity: the even-or-odd count of excitations. An $X_iX_j$ term flips two qubits, and flipping two changes the count by $-2$, $0$ or $+2$: even stays even and odd stays odd. The field terms do not flip anything. So the Hamiltonian cannot change the parity.
The proof, step by step

items: Step 1. $X_i$ anticommutes with $Z_i$: $X_iZ_i = -Z_iX_i$. It commutes with $Z_k$ for $k\ne i$, because they act on different qubits.

Step 2. Move $X_iX_j$ past $\Pi=Z_1\cdots Z_n$. Passing $X_i$ through the factor $Z_i$ gives one minus sign, passing $X_j$ through $Z_j$ gives another, and all other factors commute. Two minus signs cancel: $X_iX_j\,\Pi = \Pi\,X_iX_j$.
Step 3. $Z_i$ commutes with $\Pi$ trivially (all $Z$ operators commute). So every term of $H$ commutes with $\Pi$, hence $[H,\Pi]=0$.

blocks.text: Consequences. $\Pi$ has eigenvalues $\pm1$, so the Hilbert space splits into an even block and an odd block, each of dimension $2^{n-1}$ ($8$ for $n=4$). $H$ never connects them. If the state sits entirely in the even block, it stays there. Second, an observable that is parity-even (it commutes with $\Pi$, such as $Z_i$ and $Z_iZ_j$) has no matrix elements between the blocks, so it cannot detect coherence between an even state and an odd state. An observable such as $X_1$ is parity-odd: it anticommutes with $\Pi$ and connects the blocks.

Be careful with the word symmetry. In the full reservoir the input step (discard qubit 1, insert a fresh qubit) does not conserve parity: the inserted state $\sqrt{1-s}\vert0\rangle+\sqrt{s}\vert1\rangle$ is a superposition of both parities. Parity is a property of the Hamiltonian, and between resets it is conserved; across a reset it is not.

blocks.title: Check yourself: parity of a feature
blocks.text: The register starts in $\vert000\rangle$ and evolves under the Hamiltonian with no input and no reset. What is $\langle Z_1Z_2\rangle - \langle Z_3\rangle$ at every later time?
blocks.hint: Which basis states can ever be populated?
solution: $\vert000\rangle$ has $\Pi=(+1)^3=+1$, and $H$ conserves $\Pi$, so the state stays in the even block (basis states $\vert000\rangle,\vert011\rangle,\vert101\rangle,\vert110\rangle$).
In every even basis state $Z_1Z_2Z_3=+1$, hence $Z_1Z_2=Z_3$ (multiply both sides by $Z_3$, using $Z_3^2=1$).
So $\langle Z_1Z_2\rangle=\langle Z_3\rangle$ and the difference is 0.

blocks.text: The input step
Why we need it

Now we have a machine that moves information around. How does a number $s_k$ get in, and how does the machine ever forget? A closed quantum system never forgets: its evolution is reversible, so in principle the whole past can be run backwards out of the present. A reservoir that never forgets would still be reacting to its starting state a thousand steps later. We need one irreversible operation.
The idea

Throw away qubit 1 and put a new one in its place, in a state that depends on the input. Throwing away is the irreversible part: whatever the old qubit 1 knew about the past, including whatever was entangled with the other qubits, is cut off. The other $n-1$ qubits are not touched, so what they remember survives. The picture: a row of workers each holding a note, passing notes along the row. At every tick the first worker is replaced by a new worker holding the latest message. Notes that were already passed down the row survive; notes still with the first worker are lost.
The maths

Here $\rho_{k-1}$ is the density matrix of all $n$ qubits at the end of the previous step (a $2^n\times2^n$ matrix, see Mixed States (#/quantum/many-body/mixed-states)). $\operatorname{Tr}_1\rho_{k-1}$ is the partial trace over qubit 1: the density matrix of qubits $2,\dots,n$ alone, size $2^{n-1}\times2^{n-1}$ (see Entanglement and Reduced States (#/quantum/many-body/entanglement)). The symbol $\otimes$ glues the new qubit 1 onto it. $U=e^{-iH\Delta t}$ is the evolution for a time $\Delta t$, and $U\cdot U^\dagger$ is how it acts on a density matrix. The prepared qubit has $P(1)=s$, so the input is written into the probability of finding a one: an input $s=0.25$ gives a qubit that reads $1$ one time in four.

Written in Pauli components, the prepared state is $\tfrac12\left(I + (1-2s)Z + 2\sqrt{s(1-s)}\,X\right)$: its $Z$ component is $\langle Z\rangle = 1-2s$ and its $X$ component is $\langle X\rangle = 2\sqrt{s(1-s)}$. Check with $s=0$: $(1,0)$, the state $\vert0\rangle$. With $s=1/2$: $(0, 1)$, the state $\vert+\rangle$. With $s=1$: $(-1, 0)$, the state $\vert1\rangle$. The input enters through two functions, $1-2s$ (linear) and $2\sqrt{s(1-s)}$ (a square-root arch). These are the only functions of one input the reset can produce.
A worked example, with numbers

Two qubits, $J=0.5$, $h=1$, $\Delta t=1$, starting in $\vert00\rangle$, with inputs $s_1=0.25$, $s_2=0.8$, $s_3=0.5$. The program at the end of this section prints every number below. We do step 1 by hand using the two blocks from before.

items: Step 1. Discard qubit 1 of $\vert00\rangle\langle00\vert$: what is left is qubit 2 in $\vert0\rangle$. Insert qubit 1 in $\vert\psi_{0.25}\rangle=\sqrt{0.75}\vert0\rangle+\sqrt{0.25}\vert1\rangle$. The register is $\sqrt{0.75}\,\vert00\rangle+\sqrt{0.25}\,\vert10\rangle$. The first piece lives in block A, the second in block B.

Step 2. Evolve block A for $t=1$. $\Omega=2.0616$. The amplitude to stay in $\vert00\rangle$ is $\cos\Omega t - i\,(2h/\Omega)\sin\Omega t=-0.4713-0.8556i$ (using $\cos 2.0616=-0.4713$, $\sin2.0616=0.8820$, $2h/\Omega=0.9701$). The amplitude to reach $\vert11\rangle$ has magnitude $(J/\Omega)\sin\Omega t=0.2425\times0.8820=0.2139$. So the probabilities, times $0.75$ (the weight of this piece): $P(00)=0.75\times(0.4713^2+0.8556^2)=0.75\times0.9542=0.7157$ and $P(11)=0.75\times0.2139^2=0.0343$. The two add to $0.75$, as they must.

Step 3. Evolve block B. The state $\vert10\rangle$ turns into $\cos(Jt)\vert10\rangle - i\sin(Jt)\vert01\rangle$ with $\cos0.5=0.8776$, $\sin0.5=0.4794$. With weight $0.25$: $P(10)=0.25\times0.8776^2=0.1925$ and $P(01)=0.25\times0.4794^2=0.0575$.

Step 5 (the next input). The reduced state of qubit 2 now has $Z$ component $0.8164$ and $X$ component $0.3553$ (a coherence that came from the interference of the pieces of the register). Discard qubit 1 and insert $s_2=0.8$: $\langle Z_1\rangle$ starts at $1-2(0.8)=-0.6$. After evolution the program gives $\langle Z_1\rangle=-0.2461$ and $\langle Z_2\rangle=0.5415$. For $s_3=0.5$ the features are $-0.0193$ and $0.5044$.

blocks.source:
import numpy as np

# Two-qubit spin reservoir, H = J X1 X2 + h (Z1 + Z2), worked step by step
X = np.array([[0, 1], [1, 0]], complex); Z = np.diag([1, -1]).astype(complex); I2 = np.eye(2)
J, h, dt = 0.5, 1.0, 1.0
H = J * np.kron(X, X) + h * (np.kron(Z, I2) + np.kron(I2, Z))
print("H (real part) rows:"); print(np.round(H.real, 3))
E, P = np.linalg.eigh(H)
print("eigenvalues of H:", np.round(E, 4))
U = P @ np.diag(np.exp(-1j * E * dt)) @ P.conj().T
print("U[|11>,|00>] =", np.round(U[3, 0], 4), " |.|^2 =", round(abs(U[3, 0]) ** 2, 4))

def reduced_q2(rho):                     # Tr_1 of a 4x4 matrix
    r = rho.reshape(2, 2, 2, 2)
    return r[0, :, 0, :] + r[1, :, 1, :]

rho = np.kron(np.diag([1., 0]), np.diag([1., 0])).astype(complex)   # |00><00|
for k, s in enumerate([0.25, 0.8, 0.5], start=1):
    q2 = reduced_q2(rho)
    psi = np.array([np.sqrt(1 - s), np.sqrt(s)])
    inj = np.kron(np.outer(psi, psi), q2)
    rho = U @ inj @ U.conj().T
    z1 = np.real(np.trace(rho @ np.kron(Z, I2))); z2 = np.real(np.trace(rho @ np.kron(I2, Z)))
    print(f"step {k}: s={s}  Tr1(rho_prev) Bloch z = {np.real(q2[0,0]-q2[1,1]):+.4f}, x = {2*np.real(q2[0,1]):+.4f}"
          f"   prepared <Z1>={1-2*s:+.3f}  after evolution <Z1>={z1:+.4f}  <Z2>={z2:+.4f}")

blocks.text: Look at the features after step 2. Qubit 1 was set to $\langle Z\rangle=-0.6$ and came out at $-0.2461$: the coupling carried part of the input away to qubit 2, and brought part of qubit 2's older content back. Qubit 2 carries information about both $s_1$ and $s_2$ in $\langle Z_2\rangle=0.5415$; the readout cannot tell which from this one number, which is why we want several features, taken at several times.

Common mistake: thinking the reset means the input is written and then measured. Nobody measures qubit 1. The fresh qubit is simply inserted into the register, and its state is then part of the joint state. The only measurement is the $\langle Z_i\rangle$ readout, discussed below.

blocks.text: Why the memory fades, and what shape it has
Why we need it

The reservoir is useful only if the influence of old inputs fades (the echo state property from The Echo State Property (#/qrc/foundations/echo-state-property)), but not too fast. Where does the fading come from here, and can we say how fast?
The idea

Think of information about an old input as sitting somewhere in the register. Each step, the Hamiltonian moves some of it onto qubit 1, and the next reset deletes whatever is on qubit 1. So the information leaks out, at a rate set by how fast $H$ exchanges information between qubit 1 and the rest. If qubit 1 were completely decoupled the information would never leak and the reservoir would remember its starting state forever. If it were swapped out entirely every step there would be nothing to remember. The memory lives in between, in the qubits $2,\dots,n$ and in how slowly the reset can drain them.

In the language of Contraction and Fixed Points (#/qrc/open-systems/contraction-and-fixed-points): the map from one step to the next is a quantum channel, and for generic $H$ the distance between any two states (the trace distance, a measure of how distinguishable they are by any measurement) never increases and, after a few steps, strictly decreases. Two copies of the reservoir that start in different states but receive the same inputs converge to the same trajectory, and that convergence is the echo state property.
What nonlinearity the model offers

The step is linear in the density matrix. The prepared state is linear in the three numbers $(1,\ 1-2s,\ 2\sqrt{s(1-s)})$. So every feature $\langle Z_i\rangle_k$ is a sum of terms, each a product of one such factor per past step: for example $(1-2s_k)$, or $(1-2s_k)\cdot2\sqrt{s_{k-1}(1-s_{k-1})}$, or $\sqrt{s_{k}(1-s_k)}\sqrt{s_{k-2}(1-s_{k-2})}$. Products across time appear naturally; a pure power of a single input such as $s_k^2$ does not, because each past step contributes at most one factor. So the reservoir computes sums of products of arch-shaped functions of past inputs, and a ridge readout weights them. This is exactly the kind of structure a task such as $s_ks_{k-1}$ needs, and why a quantum reservoir with this encoding is better at memory-times-nonlinearity tasks than the plain delay: see Input Encoding (#/qrc/models/input-encoding).
What sets how long it lasts

Three things compete. The coupling scale $J$ times the step length $\Delta t$ says how far information travels between resets. If $J\Delta t\ll1$, almost nothing has left qubit 1 when it is reset, so the reservoir sees only the current input. If $J\Delta t$ is of order one or more, information spreads before the reset and memory is limited instead by the number of qubits and the leakage back to qubit 1. Finally, the number of qubits is the room available to park information away from the reset. Because the evolution between resets is unitary (nothing is lost) the reset is the only forgetting, which is why even 4 qubits and 20 features can recall several steps.
Readout and virtual nodes
Why we need it

With 4 qubits and a single reading of $\langle Z_i\rangle$ per step the readout has 4 features. A feature vector with 4 numbers can hold at most 4 independent pieces of information about the past. That is a hard ceiling: a memory capacity (the sum of the squared correlations of recalling each delay, defined in Memory and Processing Capacity (#/qrc/foundations/memory-and-capacity)) cannot exceed the number of features. How do we get more features out of the same few qubits?
The idea and the maths

Do not read only at the end of $\Delta t$. Split the evolution into $V$ equal sub-steps and record $\langle Z_i\rangle$ after each. These readings are the virtual nodes (a name borrowed from the delay-line photonic reservoirs of Physical Reservoirs (#/qrc/foundations/physical-reservoirs)). An $n$-qubit reservoir with $V$ virtual nodes gives $M=nV$ features per input. They are not copies of each other. After one sub-step the register has moved to a different state, and in the Heisenberg picture each reading measures a different operator: $U^{\dagger v}Z_iU^{v}$ for $v=1,\dots,V$. Different operators are different linear functionals of the same state, and for generic dynamics they are independent until the number of them approaches the number of independent operators the dynamics can reach.

blocks.tex: x_k = \left(\langle Z_1\rangle_{k,1},\dots,\langle Z_n\rangle_{k,1},\ \dots,\ \langle Z_1\rangle_{k,V},\dots,\langle Z_n\rangle_{k,V}\right)\in\mathbb{R}^{nV}, \qquad y_k = w_0+\sum_{i=1}^{nV}w_i\,x_{k,i}
blocks.caption: Features of step k (the notation <Z_i>_{k,v} is the reading of qubit i after the v-th sub-step of input k) and the trained linear readout.

blocks.text: In the original proposal the system is an ensemble, such as an NMR sample with a huge number of identical molecules, and a macroscopic signal gives $\langle Z_i\rangle$ directly without collapsing every copy. On a single quantum device each feature has to be estimated by repeating the experiment, and every measurement disturbs the state. This is the measurement problem treated in Measurement Back-Action and Shot Noise (#/qrc/hardware/measurement-back-action). For the simulations on this page we assume exact expectation values, and add shot noise only where we say so.
Training and scoring

items: Drive the reservoir with independent random inputs, uniform on $[0,1]$. Discard the first 200 steps (the washout) so the starting state is forgotten.

Record the features for 800 training steps and append a constant column of ones (the bias). For a target $y$ (for example the input $d$ steps back, $s_{k-d}$) solve the ridge problem $w=(F^\top F+\lambda I)^{-1}F^\top y$, as in Linear Regression and the Ridge Readout (#/qrc/start/linear-regression-and-ridge).

On the next 400 steps, never seen in training, compute the squared correlation $r^2(d)$ between the prediction and $s_{k-d}$. The curve $r^2(d)$ is the memory function; its sum over $d\ge1$ is the memory capacity, MC.

blocks.text: The full program

Here is the whole model, with 4 qubits, $h=1$, $\Delta t=10$ and $V=5$. It builds $H$, computes the one-sub-step propagator $U$ by diagonalising $H$ ($U=P\,e^{-iE\Delta t/V}P^\dagger$ where $E$ and $P$ are the eigenvalues and eigenvectors), applies the reset by a partial trace written as a sum of the two $2\times2$ diagonal blocks of the reshaped density matrix, records the features, then fits a ridge readout for each delay.

import numpy as np

# Pauli operators on n qubits (qubit 0 = leftmost tensor factor)
X = np.array([[0, 1], [1, 0]], complex); Z = np.diag([1, -1]).astype(complex)
def op(o, i, n):
    m = np.array([[1]], complex)
    for k in range(n): m = np.kron(m, o if k == i else np.eye(2))
    return m

n, h, dt, V = 4, 1.0, 10.0, 5          # qubits, field, time per input, virtual nodes
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
H = sum(rng.uniform(-0.5, 0.5) * op(X, i, n) @ op(X, j, n) for i in range(n) for j in range(i + 1, n))
H = H + h * sum(op(Z, i, n) for i in range(n))
E, P = np.linalg.eigh(H)
U = P @ np.diag(np.exp(-1j * E * dt / V)) @ P.conj().T       # one virtual-node step
D = 2 ** n
zdiag = [np.real(np.diag(op(Z, i, n))) for i in range(n)]

def features(s):
    rho = np.eye(D) / D
    out = []
    for x in s:
        r4 = rho.reshape(2, D // 2, 2, D // 2)
        rest = r4[0, :, 0, :] + r4[1, :, 1, :]                 # Tr_1 rho
        psi = np.array([np.sqrt(1 - x), np.sqrt(x)])
        rho = np.kron(np.outer(psi, psi), rest)                 # reset qubit 1 to the input state
        f = []
        for _ in range(V):
            rho = U @ rho @ U.conj().T
            d = np.real(np.diag(rho))
            f += [z @ d for z in zdiag]                        # <Z_i>
        out.append(f)
    return np.array(out)

s = np.random.default_rng(101).uniform(0, 1, 1400)
F = np.hstack([features(s), np.ones((len(s), 1))])
wash, tr = 200, 800
mc = 0.0
for d in range(0, 13):
    A, y = F[wash:wash + tr], s[wash - d:wash + tr - d]
    w = np.linalg.solve(A.T @ A + 1e-6 * np.eye(A.shape[1]), A.T @ y)
    r2 = np.corrcoef(F[wash + tr:] @ w, s[wash + tr - d:len(s) - d])[0, 1] ** 2
    if d > 0: mc += r2
    print(f"d={d:2d}  r2={r2:.3f}")
print(f"memory capacity (d=1..12): {mc:.2f}")

blocks.text: Run as written, the program gives $r^2=0.996$ for the current input ($d=0$), $0.942$ at $d=1$, $0.817$ at $d=2$, $0.676$ at $d=3$, $0.582$ at $d=4$, and almost nothing from $d=10$. The memory capacity over delays 1 to 12 is 3.75, out of a ceiling of $nV=20$ features. The JavaScript simulator below is the same model with different random draws, so its numbers differ by a few tenths.

widget.title: Memory function of the spin reservoir

blocks.text: Try this. (1) Leave the defaults (4 qubits, $V=1$): the label reads MC of about 2.1 from only 4 features. (2) Set $V$ to 5: MC rises to about 5.1; the extra features are the same qubits seen at different times during the evolution, and they are independent because the dynamics rotates information through the register. (3) Keep $V=5$ and set shots to 100: MC falls to about 1.9, below the exact $V=1$ result; each feature now carries noise of order $0.1$ and the readout can no longer separate the small contributions of old inputs. At 1000 shots MC is about 3.3. (4) Set disorder $W$ to 5 with $V=5$ and shots 0: MC falls from about 5.1 to about 4.1 as the qubits detune from each other; much stronger disorder kills the memory, as the Dynamical Regimes (#/qrc/models/dynamical-regimes) page shows.

blocks.title: Check yourself: feature count
blocks.text: A reservoir has 5 qubits and 8 virtual nodes. How many features does the readout have, and what is the largest memory capacity it can possibly show?
blocks.hint: Features per input are qubits times virtual nodes.
solution: MC is the sum of squared correlations $r^2(d)\le1$ over delays, and a linear readout of $M$ independent features can recall at most $M$ independent inputs, so MC $\le40$ (the same bound as Jaeger's for classical networks).
In practice the features are far from independent recall channels and MC is much smaller (3.75 of 20 above).

blocks.text: What sets the memory: a sweep
Why we need it
The model has knobs: the number of qubits $n$, the step length $\Delta t$, and $V$. The rule of thumb above (three competing time scales) is only useful if you can see it. So let us measure it.
The experiment

The program below uses the same model and the same random couplings (seed 1) and varies $\Delta t$ and $n$ with a single reading per step ($V=1$), then varies $V$ at $n=4$. It prints the memory capacity for delays 1 to 12. This is one draw of the couplings, so every entry could shift by a few tenths with another draw.

blocks.source:
import numpy as np

X = np.array([[0, 1], [1, 0]], complex); Z = np.diag([1, -1]).astype(complex)
def op(o, i, n):
    m = np.array([[1]], complex)
    for k in range(n): m = np.kron(m, o if k == i else np.eye(2))
    return m

def memory_capacity(n, dt, V, h=1.0, seed=1, dmax=12):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed); D = 2 ** n
    H = sum(rng.uniform(-0.5, 0.5) * op(X, i, n) @ op(X, j, n) for i in range(n) for j in range(i + 1, n))
    H = H + h * sum(op(Z, i, n) for i in range(n))
    E, P = np.linalg.eigh(H); U = P @ np.diag(np.exp(-1j * E * dt / V)) @ P.conj().T
    zd = [np.real(np.diag(op(Z, i, n))) for i in range(n)]
    s = np.random.default_rng(101).uniform(0, 1, 1400); rho = np.eye(D) / D; F = []
    for x in s:
        r4 = rho.reshape(2, D // 2, 2, D // 2); rest = r4[0, :, 0, :] + r4[1, :, 1, :]
        psi = np.array([np.sqrt(1 - x), np.sqrt(x)]); rho = np.kron(np.outer(psi, psi), rest); f = []
        for _ in range(V):
            rho = U @ rho @ U.conj().T; d = np.real(np.diag(rho)); f += [z @ d for z in zd]
        F.append(f)
    F = np.hstack([np.array(F), np.ones((len(s), 1))]); wash, tr = 200, 800; mc = 0
    for d in range(1, dmax + 1):
        A = F[wash:wash + tr]; y = s[wash - d:wash + tr - d]
        w = np.linalg.solve(A.T @ A + 1e-6 * np.eye(A.shape[1]), A.T @ y)
        mc += np.corrcoef(F[wash + tr:] @ w, s[wash + tr - d:len(s) - d])[0, 1] ** 2
    return mc

print("MC (delays 1-12), V=1, h=1, one random draw (seed 1)")
print("  dt:      " + "  ".join(f"{dt:5g}" for dt in (0.5, 1, 2, 5, 10, 20)))
for n in (2, 3, 4, 5):
    print(f"  n={n} qubits: " + "  ".join(f"{memory_capacity(n, dt, 1):5.2f}" for dt in (0.5, 1, 2, 5, 10, 20)))
print("n=4, dt=10, as the virtual nodes V grow (features = 4V):")
print("  " + "  ".join(f"V={V}: {memory_capacity(4, 10, V):.2f}" for V in (1, 2, 3, 5, 8)))

blocks.text: Reading the table. For $n=2$ the memory is tiny at every $\Delta t$ (below $0.7$): with only one coupling and a single reset qubit, two features are all there is, and the sample draw has a weak coupling, so it needs a very long $\Delta t$ before much information moves. For $n=3$ and $4$ the capacity peaks at short $\Delta t$ (1 to 2) with $V=1$ and then falls and wanders at longer times: after a long evolution the register has been scrambled so thoroughly that qubit 1 has re-absorbed most of what it knew and the reset deletes it. More qubits help: at $\Delta t=1$ MC rises from $1.84$ to $2.43$ to $3.83$ for $n=3,4,5$. And with $n=4$, $\Delta t=10$, more virtual nodes help steadily: MC is $1.42$ at $V=1$, $2.13$ at $V=2$, $3.11$ at $V=3$, $3.75$ at $V=5$ and $4.62$ at $V=8$.
The simplest summary: memory needs features, and features come from qubits and from sampling times. The Hilbert-space dimension $2^n$ does not enter directly.

A frequent misreading: the $2^n$ dimension is not the memory capacity. An $n$-qubit state has $4^n-1$ real numbers, but a linear readout of $M$ observables exposes at most $M$ independent combinations, and each must be estimated from finite shots. Growing the reservoir helps only together with a readout that grows with it.

blocks.title: Check yourself: reading the sweep
blocks.text: Using the table, which has the better memory per feature: $n=5$, $\Delta t=1$, $V=1$, or $n=4$, $\Delta t=10$, $V=5$? Give MC divided by the number of features for each.
solution: The short-$\Delta t$ five-qubit reservoir is four times more efficient per feature here, though the second needs only four qubits. Which is cheaper depends on whether qubits or readouts are scarcer.

blocks.text: Putting it together

Problem. You are given a 4-qubit device with couplings of about $J\sim0.5$ and can choose the step length $\Delta t$ and the number of readouts per step. You need to recall the input from 3 steps ago with $r^2$ above $0.6$ and you can afford at most 12 feature readings per step. Use what the page taught to choose settings and predict the outcome, then test the prediction.

items: Step 1. Budget. $12=nV=4V$ gives $V=3$ virtual nodes at four qubits. Twelve features can in principle carry 12 independent pieces of the past; we need only one delay, so the bound is not the problem.

Step 2. Time scale. The sweep above (for $V=1$) says the memory is poor when $\Delta t$ is very short ($J\Delta t\ll1$: MC $0.97$ at $\Delta t=0.5$) and falls again when $\Delta t$ is very long (MC $1.42$ at $\Delta t=10$), with the best values in between ($2.43$ at $\Delta t=1$, $2.27$ at $2$). So try $\Delta t$ of order 1 to 5 rather than 10.

Step 3. Predict. With three virtual nodes the features double or triple relative to $V=1$, so I expect $r^2(3)$ clearly above $0.6$ at $\Delta t=2$, and I am not sure about $\Delta t=10$ (the full run above got $0.676$ with 20 features there).

Step 4. Test. The program below runs the four candidates. At $\Delta t=2$, $V=3$ the recall of $s_{k-3}$ has $r^2=0.90$, comfortably above $0.6$. At $\Delta t=10$, $V=3$ it is $0.569$, just below. The same 12 features do better when the step is shorter.

blocks.source:
import numpy as np

X = np.array([[0, 1], [1, 0]], complex); Z = np.diag([1, -1]).astype(complex)
def op(o, i, n):
    m = np.array([[1]], complex)
    for k in range(n): m = np.kron(m, o if k == i else np.eye(2))
    return m

def r2_by_delay(n,dt,V,seed=1,h=1.0):
    rng=np.random.default_rng(seed); D=2**n
    H=sum(rng.uniform(-.5,.5)*op(X,i,n)@op(X,j,n) for i in range(n) for j in range(i+1,n))+h*sum(op(Z,i,n) for i in range(n))
    E,P=np.linalg.eigh(H); U=P@np.diag(np.exp(-1j*E*dt/V))@P.conj().T
    zd=[np.real(np.diag(op(Z,i,n))) for i in range(n)]
    s=np.random.default_rng(101).uniform(0,1,1400); rho=np.eye(D)/D; F=[]
    for x in s:
        r4=rho.reshape(2,D//2,2,D//2); rest=r4[0,:,0,:]+r4[1,:,1,:]
        psi=np.array([np.sqrt(1-x),np.sqrt(x)]); rho=np.kron(np.outer(psi,psi),rest); f=[]
        for _ in range(V):
            rho=U@rho@U.conj().T; d=np.real(np.diag(rho)); f+=[z@d for z in zd]
        F.append(f)
    F=np.hstack([np.array(F),np.ones((len(s),1))]); wash,tr=200,800; out=[]
    for d in range(1,6):
        A=F[wash:wash+tr]; y=s[wash-d:wash+tr-d]
        w=np.linalg.solve(A.T@A+1e-6*np.eye(A.shape[1]),A.T@y)
        out.append(np.corrcoef(F[wash+tr:]@w,s[wash+tr-d:len(s)-d])[0,1]**2)
    return np.round(out,3)

print("n=4, h=1, one draw: r^2 of recalling s(k-d) for d = 1..5")
for dt, V in [(2, 3), (10, 3), (1, 3), (5, 3)]:
    print(f"  dt={dt:<3} V={V} ({4*V} features): ", r2_by_delay(4, dt, V))

blocks.text: Two lessons from the output. The procedure is: count features, choose a time scale from the competition between $J\Delta t$ and the number of qubits, predict, test. And the outcome is not monotonic: at $\Delta t=1$ the recall of $s_{k-5}$ ($r^2=0.67$) is better than at $\Delta t=2$ ($0.22$), but the recall at $d=1$ is worse. These are single draws of the couplings, so treat differences of a few tenths between neighbouring settings as noise and the broad trend (short beats long) as the finding.
Key points

items: The spin-network reservoir is $H=\sum_{i<j}J_{ij}X_iX_j+\sum_ih_iZ_i$ with fixed random $J_{ij}$; the couplings move information between qubits and the field makes the dynamics non-commuting so it mixes.
The Hamiltonian conserves the parity $Z_1\cdots Z_n$ (two sign flips cancel), so $H$ splits into two blocks of size $2^{n-1}$ and parity-even observables ignore parity-odd coherences.
Input step: discard qubit 1, insert $\sqrt{1-s}\vert0\rangle+\sqrt{s}\vert1\rangle$ (Bloch components $1-2s$ and $2\sqrt{s(1-s)}$), evolve for $\Delta t$ with $U=e^{-iH\Delta t}$.
The reset is the only dissipation: it deletes what is on qubit 1, and the memory is whatever the other qubits keep and how slowly it leaks back.
Features are products of one factor per past input; there are no pure powers of a single input.
Virtual nodes give $M=nV$ features per input; MC is bounded by $M$ and depends on $J\Delta t$ and $n$, not on $2^n$.
Shot noise cuts the memory sharply: 100 shots per feature drops MC from 5.1 to 1.9 in the simulator.

blocks.text: Problems

blocks.title: The prepared input state
blocks.text: For $s=0.25$, give $\langle Z\rangle$ and $\langle X\rangle$ of $\vert\psi_s\rangle$, and the probability of measuring 1.

blocks.title: Detuning stops hopping
blocks.text: Two qubits coupled by $J X_1X_2$ with $h_1Z_1+h_2Z_2$ (different fields) start in $\vert10\rangle$. In the odd block $\{\vert01\rangle,\vert10\rangle\}$ the matrix has diagonal $\pm(h_1-h_2)$ and off-diagonal $J$. With $J=0.25$, what is the largest probability of finding the excitation on qubit 2 for $h_1-h_2=0$, $0.5$ and $5$?
blocks.hint: This is the two-level formula from the worked example.
solution: Differences between qubits' fields (disorder) switch off the exchange: the next pages use this to explain why strong disorder destroys memory.

blocks.title: Reading the memory function
blocks.text: The sample prints $r^2(d)$ = 0.942, 0.817, 0.676, 0.582 for $d=1$ to 4 and a total MC of 3.75 for $d=1$ to 12. What fraction of the capacity comes from delays 1 to 4, and what is the ceiling on MC with this readout?
blocks.hint: Add the four values and divide by the total.
solution: Ceiling: $M=nV=4\times5=20$ features. The reservoir uses under a fifth of it: the features are far from independent recall channels, because the readout must also undo the nonlinear mixing of each past input.

blocks.title: Shots and the readout
blocks.text: A feature $\langle Z_1\rangle\approx0.5$ is estimated from $S=100$ shots. What is its standard error, and how many shots would be needed for $0.01$?
solution: Variance of one shot: $1-\langle Z\rangle^2=0.75$. Standard error $\sqrt{0.75/100}=0.0866$.
An error of $0.087$ per feature is comparable to the contribution of an input five steps back, which is why 100 shots destroy the long-delay memory in the widget.

blocks.text: Where this is used

The next four pages each change one choice of this model. Input Encoding (#/qrc/models/input-encoding) changes how the number $s_k$ is written into qubit 1 (and shows why the parity symmetry makes some encodings invisible). Readout and Multiplexing (#/qrc/models/readout-and-multiplexing) changes what is measured and how often. Dynamical Regimes (#/qrc/models/dynamical-regimes) changes the couplings and the field to ask when the reservoir is ergodic, integrable or localised. Dissipation as a Resource (#/qrc/models/dissipation-as-resource) replaces the reset by genuine loss. On the hardware shelf the same model reappears as a protocol to be run on a real device, with the measurement cost made explicit.
